title: The Lies We Live By: You're Enough (Part 1)
speaker: Pastor Tito Lyro
summary: Pastor Tito Lyro examines the popular cultural lie that "you are enough," demonstrating through Scripture how this message contradicts biblical anthropology and the gospel. He shows that humans were created to be dependent on God's revelation, to interpret life through God's framework, and to worship God—not themselves—and therefore cannot function adequately apart from Him.

outline.title: Introduction to the Series: Why We Believe Lies
subpoints: Lies are packaged attractively and widely accepted without critical examination
We believe lies through cultural pressure, pragmatism, weariness, laziness, and desire to fit in
The series challenges false doctrines embraced by Christians in American culture
Previous lies examined: Follow your heart, trust your instinct, live your truth

outline.title: The Lie: You Are Enough
subpoints: This message is hopeless—it burdens people with self-sufficiency when they are overwhelmed
The gospel contradicts this: you are not enough; Christ is enough for you
Self-esteem is another label for this doctrine, promoted especially since mid-20th century
This lie assumes people are basically good, but Scripture and experience prove otherwise
The doctrine produces self-centered, selfish people unable to work together

outline.title: The Design of Humanity: Three Foundational Truths
subpoints: Humans are created to be revelation receivers—dependent on God's word, not self-sufficient
Even Adam and Eve in perfection needed God's guidance and instruction
Humans are interpreters who need God's framework for valid interpretation of life
Without God's word as our lens, we cannot see the world or ourselves correctly

outline.title: Humans as Worshippers by Nature
subpoints: Everything humans do expresses worship of something
We are either worshipping God properly or worshipping ourselves or serving idols
The self-esteem movement has created widespread self-worship
Humility means thinking of yourself less, not thinking less of yourself
Self-worship demands to be the center of the universe, creating conflict

outline.title: Our Natural Rebellion Against Dependence
subpoints: By nature, people want to get their own way and resist God's authority
The lie 'you are enough' appeals to our desire for independence
Yet we cannot exist apart from God being in charge of our lives
The tension between our desire for autonomy and our created need for dependence on God

transcript:
## Introduction to the Series: The Lies We Live By

We'll continue our series that we started four weeks ago on lies that we live by. These are things that we willingly accept, sometimes perhaps not even willingly, but unknowingly accept and live by. We often believe in lies without even knowing that we do. Ideas are packaged in such a way that they look shiny and attractive, and we tend to gravitate toward them.

We assume that a concept is true because it is being pushed by everyone around us. We tend to think of truth as dictated by a majority. Or we think that something is right because it works. The United States embraces a particular school of philosophy—not a brick and mortar place that people go to study, but an ideology. There's really only one school of philosophy that was actually creating a nice state, and that is pragmatism. Whatever works is what determines whether it's right or wrong, whether it's true or not, and we bind to those things sometimes.

Sometimes we believe lies because we want to fit in. Standing for what is true can be tiring. It can bring you down, it can be a burden to always be standing for what is true, especially in this area of the country where darkness seems to be greater and greater, and it just wears you down. Sometimes we give in and start living according to lies just because we're plain old tired.

Another reason we believe in lies and live by them is that perhaps we can be a little too lazy to actually think through things and just take whatever is offered to us. We don't think things through. In this series we're trying to challenge lies that have been unwittingly, sometimes even deliberately embraced by Christians in our culture, specifically American culture and in more liberal places like ours.

My desire for us is to have our eyes open to false notions in our own lives so that we can in turn also help others see that. It's a Matthew 7 sort of thing. Jesus says first take that plank out of your own eye before you can help somebody else with their speck. What lies are we believing that we need to repent of? That can actually be effective instruments in God's hand in blessing others.

## The Gospel Lies of Our Culture

These are the kinds of ideas that we're talking about. We started looking at them three or four weeks ago. A lot of these things are treated as gospel truths in our society:

- Follow your heart
- Trust your instinct; they never lie
- Live your truth
- You are enough
- You should put yourself first
- You only live once (YOLO)
- God just wants you to be happy
- You shouldn't judge
- You are the boss of you
- It's all about love
- Believe in yourself; you're perfect just as you are

Some of these are not mutually exclusive lies. Some of these are just different ways of saying the same thing. What's troubling is that some of these lies have been extracted from Christian literature, not just from self-help books, but from Christian literature. These things are being sold to Christians and by Christians as well.

## Previous Lies Examined

So far we've looked at the first one: follow your heart. We saw that the heart is corrupt and desperately wicked. We also addressed the second one: trust your instinct; they never lie. That's just a different way to say follow your heart. And then we looked at the idea of live your truth. Just live your truth. Be you. That's not what we were saying—you do you. There's no such thing as my truth and your truth. There is the truth and then lies.

Now, we sometimes use this language to talk about opinions. What is the best dessert? Well, those are going to be opinions, right? So it's not your truth and my truth; it's my opinion and your opinion. There's only one truth. We might have different opinions, but there's just one truth.

## The Lie: You Are Enough

Tonight, I would like to examine another claim that is very popular in our culture, and that is the claim that you are enough. You are enough.

Rachel Hollis, in her book titled *Girls, Wash Your Face: Stop Believing Lies About Who You Are So You Can Become Who You Were Meant to Be*, says this: "I studied the gospel and finally grasped the divine knowledge that I am loved and worthy and enough as I am." When you read that, you expect that as you keep reading, she would say something about being loved and worthy and enough because of her union with Christ. She has been studying the gospel, right? That's how she starts there. But as you keep on reading, you see that what she means is exactly like she stated: she's loved, worthy, and enough in and of herself. She is enough just by herself, just the way she is.

Now, why even spend time talking about this? Well, because the message that you're enough is a hopeless message. We all know that we are not enough. At least we know that we're not enough 100% of the time. Is that fair to say? I hope we all can think of a time when we came to a realization that we weren't enough for a particular thing, or a situation where we weren't enough. We all have been in situations where we know that we're not enough. This is fair. We face difficulty, difficult decisions, health crises. And to be told that we are enough just makes a tough situation even tougher.

You're in the pit of despair and it's all you're told is "you're enough. You're sufficient in and of yourself." When you've been trying to climb out of that pit of despair by yourself, that's a hopeless message. It's a message that enslaves people to the false idea that they are responsible to be the mastermind of their current circumstances and future realities, even when they are completely overwhelmed by life.

It burdens us with the obligation of being the source of our own joy, contentment, and peace because after all, you're enough. You don't need anything else; you're enough. So this is a message of despair, hopelessness. All that this idea does is make us selfish, self-reliant, and self-focused because you're enough. You don't need anything else or anybody else.

## The Gospel Contradicts This Lie

Rachel Hollis says that she studied the gospel and came to this conclusion. The problem with that conclusion is that the gospel is about somebody else. You can't study the gospel and arrive at the conclusion that you are enough because of the gospel. By definition, the gospel says that you are not enough and that somebody else—Jesus Christ—is enough for both of you.

What is another way to talk about this idea that you're enough? Which is actually more common in our society? Another gift of the baby boomers, because they keep on giving. The idea is self-esteem. Another label for the "you are enough" doctrine is self-esteem. In the middle to late twentieth century—which is why I say it's another gift of the baby boomers—Christians embraced the idea of self-esteem. We have been conditioned to think that if we just love ourselves more, everything will get better.

And we're starting to reap the harvest of an almost entire generation being raised in this idea: everybody's special, everybody's a winner, trophies for everybody. That's all wrapped up in this idea of you are enough and self-esteem. And we're creating a society that's not able to work with one another. That eventually will be the destruction of Western society, I think. Because a society that's all about self-density and the individual will not persevere, will not perpetuate itself.

The reason people say that you're supposed to love yourself more and then everything will get better is that the "you are enough" doctrine is based on the assumption that people are basically good. Now, I'm not talking about the big bad world out there. I'm talking about these ideas in Christian literature, best-selling Christian literature. But if that were true, all we would need to do is to do a deep dive into our own hearts and tap into all the virtue just waiting to be discovered there. We could pull from our unlimited reservoir of creativity, power, beauty, truth, and goodness because we are enough. And that could be the solution for everything. If all of this were true, then when someone was struggling with his or her identity, worth, or even so-called mental health issues, we should indeed point out to him or to her how wonderful they are. Just keep on telling them how great they are.

The problem is that doesn't work. But we bought into that. In a May 2021 survey, 81% of Americans believe that this would be the solution to their problems. People just need to tell them that they are great, that they are enough, and that would be the solution. 81% of Americans. And in the same survey, over 50% of Americans think that they are the greatest person they ever know—better than anybody else in their lives.

In 25 years of ministry, I have only found one person willing to say that about themselves. One man who said that as a father, he never made a mistake in his life in raising his kids. That's the only person who was actually willing to say that. I mean, there's a lot of people that believe that about themselves, but it's only one person willing to actually say it.

But deep down, we know that humans aren't basically good. Parents are keenly aware of that about themselves and about their kids. I don't think there is one—again, outside this one man—who truly thinks that they did everything right with their kids. I tend to keep on praying to the Lord and thanking Him for overwriting me more often than the other way. There's often a sense of failure as parents. I don't know if you ever felt that, but if you haven't, it's coming.

But parents also know that they don't need to teach their kids to misbehave. You don't say, "Now, Johnny, here's how I want you to lie. I don't want to, Dad. I don't know how. Let me teach you how." That doesn't happen. We don't need to teach kids to lie. They don't need to teach them to be selfish. All parents have had the universal experience of a child who is 100% uninterested in a toy until another child wants to play with it, and then it's the most precious toy that child ever saw—enough to start World War III in your living room.

So we know that deep down, humans aren't basically good. The "you are enough" doctrine produces self-centered, selfish people, and the self-esteem and self-help movement can't explain why. We've been telling people they're so great all their lives, and yet they have all these troubles. They're selfish, and they can't work well with others. Why? Why is that going on?

Well, the reason it doesn't work is the very design of humanity. The Bible teaches that humanity was created in the image of God to live in dependence on Him.

## Humanity's Created Design

We have a super familiar passage that we tend to miss because the entire book of Genesis is so familiar to us. So here we have Genesis 1:26 through 1:28 where God is creating humanity, and then there's expanded in chapter 2. And it says this:

> "Then God said, 'Let us make man in our image, according to our likeness; let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the air, and over the cattle, over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.' So God created man in his own image, in the image of God he created him; male and female created them. Then God blessed them, and God said to them, 'Be fruitful and multiply; fill the earth and subdue it; have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the air, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.'" (Genesis 1:26-28)

There is a radical thing that we miss because this passage is so familiar. If you read Genesis 1, there's a cadence in the account of creation. Remember how it goes? Day one: God creates light. He says that it's good, and there's evening and morning of the first day. Day two: God creates heaven and earth, land and water. He says it's good, and there's evening and morning of the second day. Days three, four, five—God creates something, He says it is good, and the beat goes on.

But then He decides to create people, humans. What happens when He decides to create humans? Humans are created on day six. Somewhere into the sixth day, this pattern is going on, and all of a sudden something changes. What does that change? What does God do differently in this passage, especially at the last verse? He talks to them. He didn't talk to the moon. He didn't talk to the birds. He didn't talk to the waters or the oceans. But now He talks to them. Why did God talk to them? Why did God talk with them?

What are some thoughts? Why did God talk to them? Well, humans could talk back to Him. God could communicate with them in a way He couldn't with the rest of creation. What else? There's a different relationship between God and humanity because they're created in God's image. What else? Could it be that He talked to them because they needed God to talk to them?

I think that's a good assumption, right? God knew that even though Adam and Eve were perfect people living in a perfect relationship with Him, they could not figure out life on their own. And God needed to talk with them. They were created to be dependent. This is before sin, by the way. That shows that we would still need God's counseling, even if we were sinners. Adam and Eve needed counseling to figure out what they were supposed to do. God had to explain who they were and what they were to do with their lives. They didn't need help because they were sinners. They needed help because they were human.

This is really the first instance of ministry in human history. And it comes from God to the people He created. The wonderful counselor comes to human beings and defines their identity and purpose. And why couldn't Adam and Eve live without this? I'll give you three reasons.

### Reason One: Humans Are Created to Be Revelation Receivers

First one: Adam and Eve were created to be revelation receivers. Humanity were created to be revelation receivers. They were given the ability to communicate that no other creature was given. They were created with the ability to hear, understand, and apply God's word to their lives. And these abilities were not given primarily to encourage human relationships. They were given primarily to encourage worship with God in the vertical sense. They were given so that we could know God and understand Him.

The reciprocation doesn't need these abilities. And I think we know that intrinsically. I hope none of us go to our backyard and start talking to the pine tree or whatever bushes you have. Maybe you sing to your tomato trees to help them grow. Maybe that helps. I think we have somebody guilty of that right here. We don't go to the backyard and try to have a theological discussion with the pine tree or whatever bush you may have in your backyard, because we know the bush brings glory to God by just being there.

But humans need God's word to live fully for His glory. Our culture tends to think that we need help because of something we did or something was done to us. But the truth is that our need for help preceded sin. We are created to be dependent on God and to receive revelation from Him. So trying to live without God's help is to assign ourselves a subhuman existence. But the "you are enough" doctrine puts people in a subhuman existence—a level where you don't need God, where you don't need to have God speak in your life through His word. So you're not human. Are you following?

I'm not saying some people are physically transforming into something else. I'm just saying that the category of a person who doesn't need God and revelation from God doesn't exist in the Bible. To be human is to need to receive guidance from God. So to live without that is to live like an animal, as if we were something other than what we are.

Humans are created to live on the platform of God's revelation, which is why we're given the unique ability to communicate. So the doctrine that says "you are enough" is not good. It's not true because you were created to be a revelation receiver, to need that from God.

### Reason Two: Humans Are Created to Be Interpreters

Second, Adam and Eve were created to be interpreters. That is to say that humans are created to think. We are thinking beings. That's what homo sapiens means in Latin—the thinking man. We don't just take the bare facts of life as they are and live by them. We're meaning makers. We live our lives according to our own interpretation of facts.

When we say that God designed humans to be interpreters, we're getting at the heart of why humans do what they do. Our thinking conditions our emotions, our sense of identity, our view of others, our way of solving our problems, our willingness to receive counsel from others. And that is why we need a framework for generating valid interpretations that help us respond to life appropriately. And that framework is the word of God. Only the word of our creator can give us that framework to help us live as interpreters.

The framework is what helps us to see everything properly. It's our world. It's the lenses through which we see the world. And we need that from God. So to say that you're enough apart from anything God gives you is a lie.

### Reason Three: Humans Are Created to Be Worshippers

Here's the third thing: Adam and Eve were created to be worshippers. Some have suggested that instead of homo sapiens, it would be more biblically accurate if our species would be called homo adorans—the worshipping man. We were created so that everything in our lives drew its meaning and purpose from the person, presence, and purpose of God.

Because of this design, everything that a person does expresses worship. Do you get that? Everything that you and I do expresses worship—whatever that thing is. What you do and the way you do it express your desire to serve something. Humans cannot be divided into those who worship and those who don't. If you're a human, you worship. Every person that ever lived has been a worshipper. The problem is that the fall has distorted this creative design as well, and we are often stealing worship.

And when you say you're enough, guess who you're worshipping? Yourself. Myself. Because we are worshippers by nature, we're always either giving proper worship to God or serving something else or, more likely, worshipping ourselves. Those are the only three choices. And this idea of self-esteem, of loving yourself, of thinking of yourself as the best is self-worship.

Does anybody think I just want us to think of ourselves as the worst thing ever? You just want us to think of ourselves as miserable? No. What I want is for us to forget about thinking of ourselves altogether. Forget any of the things that are behind. Press forward to the mark of the high calling that we have in the gospel.

C.S. Lewis, though not one of us—he's not a Bible-believing evangelical—had some things to say. One of the things he said is that humility is not thinking less of yourself; it's thinking of yourself less. Don't be so consumed with thinking about you. That's what we are really after here. And self-worship is the demand to be the center of our own universe. That's what the doctrine of self-esteem has created now for a couple decades of being taught in our public schools. We have people now that are adults, and they demand to be the center of everyone's universe.

The problem is that universe can only have one center. That's mathematically proven. You can only have one center, not multiple. And that's going to create a lot of trouble, right? Because they have all these centers now vying for that privileged position.

But we're not even to the fall in the book of Genesis. Adam and Eve were created to respond to God's revelation in worship because of the God-ward reference in them. And that is part of being made in God's image—to need God's revelation, to be interpreters based on God's revelation, and then to worship God in response to God's revelation.

So you're not enough. You're not enough. You need the Lord Jesus Christ in your life.

## Our Natural Resistance to Dependence

The Bible teaches that people naturally by nature want to get their own way, serve their own desires, and resist letting God be in charge of their lives. That's why the idea of "you are enough" is so appealing because we don't want to be dependent on anybody else. We want to, like Frank Sinatra's song says, do it our own way, right? And that's kind of all of us. That's our actual desire. And we resist letting God be in charge of our lives.

Yet we can't exist apart from God being in charge of our lives. We're going to stop here. Next week we're going to start with examining how the Bible deals with our true condition since the fall and how we are not enough. If we haven't gotten that through yet, Lord willing, we can get that through next week.
